title: Largest Block Under a Bar Chart
statement:
A bar chart has bars of width 1 standing side by side with no gaps. Bar i has height heights[i].

Return the area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars. The rectangle can span several neighbouring bars, but its height is limited by the shortest bar it covers.

examples.why: The tallest bar alone gives 3 and the full width gives 5 × 1 = 5. The best is the last three bars at height 2: 3 × 2 = 6. Neither "tallest" nor "widest" wins.
Equal heights: the rectangle covers all bars. Equal neighbours must not cut a rectangle short.
A bar of height 0 splits the chart. The answer is the pair 5 and 6 at height 5.

hints: Every best rectangle is as tall as some bar it covers. Fix that bar: how far left and right can the rectangle stretch?
It stretches until the first strictly shorter bar on each side. So the problem is "nearest shorter bar to the left and to the right" for every bar.

Keep a stack of bar indices with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar it pops has just found its right limit, and the bar below it on the stack is its left limit. Compute the area as you pop.

explain.intuition:
Take the best rectangle. Its top edge touches some bar, the shortest one it covers. So try every bar as "the shortest one": the rectangle with that height extends left and right until it hits a shorter bar. The answer is the best of those n rectangles. What remains is finding, for each bar, the nearest shorter bar on both sides.

A stack of indices with increasing heights gives both at once. When bar i is shorter than the top, the top cannot extend past i: its right limit is found. Its left limit is the bar right under it on the stack, because everything between them was taller and already popped. Each bar is pushed and popped once, so the whole thing is O(n). A height-0 sentinel at the end flushes the bars still on the stack.
steps: Walk i from 0 to n, treating position n as a bar of height 0.
While the stack is not empty and heights[top] >= h, where h is the current height: pop top.
The popped bar's rectangle reaches from just after the new top (or from 0 if the stack is empty) to i − 1. Its width is i − newTop − 1 (or i); update the best area with heights[top] × width.
pitfalls: Forgetting to process the bars left on the stack at the end. An increasing chart like [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] never pops anything during the walk.
Measuring the width from the popped index instead of from the element now under it. Taller bars that were popped earlier still belong to this rectangle.
Expecting two pointers to work as in the water-container problem. The height here is the minimum over the whole span, not just the two ends.

solutions.title: Every start, running minimum
solutions.idea: Fix the left edge and move the right edge outward, keeping the minimum height covered so far.

solutions.title: Nearest shorter bar on each side
solutions.idea: Two passes with a stack: one finds the nearest strictly shorter bar on the left of each bar, the other on the right. Each bar's rectangle lies between them.

solutions.title: One pass with an increasing stack
solutions.idea: Keep indices with increasing heights. A shorter bar pops the taller ones and closes their rectangles right away; a height-0 bar at the end closes the rest.

followups: Find the largest rectangle of 1s in a 0/1 grid. How can each row become a bar chart?
Why is it fine to pop on >= even though equal bars could extend the rectangle further? Which bar ends up computing the full width?
